questions.q: What root cause do SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) share?
options: Both exist because unsanitized user input was trusted and used in a place that could change the application's behavior
Both require the attacker to already have a valid database password
Both only affect mobile applications, never web applications
Both are physical attacks that require access to the server hardware
questions.explain: Trusting input instead of validating or sanitizing it is the single design mistake behind both attack types.

questions.q: What does SQL injection actually manipulate?
options: The logic and structure of a database query, not just the data within it
The physical hard drive storing the database
Only the visual formatting of a web page
The user's own local device settings
questions.explain: Unsanitized input inserted directly into a query can alter the query's logic, such as making a condition evaluate as true regardless of actual values.

questions.q: Where does the malicious script execute in a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attack?
options: In the browser of other users who view the compromised page, not in the attacker's own browser
Only on the web server's own operating system
Only inside the attacker's personal browser, never anyone else's
Nowhere — XSS has no actual code execution involved
questions.explain: XSS is dangerous specifically because the script runs in another user's browser, inheriting that browser's trust in the site.

questions.q: What defense specifically closes off SQL injection at the database layer?
options: Parameterized queries, which keep a query's structure separate from the data plugged into it
Encrypting the entire hard drive the database runs on
Disabling all user login forms permanently
Increasing the server's available memory
questions.explain: Parameterized queries prevent user-supplied data from being interpreted as part of the query's logic, which is the core of the attack.

questions.q: A comment field stores and redisplays whatever a user submits, without sanitizing it, and an attacker submits a comment containing script instead of plain text. What vulnerability does this create?
options: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), because the unsanitized content is rendered as executable code to other viewers
SQL injection, because any user input is automatically SQL injection
A Denial of Service attack, because the comment field is now unavailable
ARP spoofing, because the local network's MAC mappings are affected
questions.explain: Displaying unsanitized submitted content as live code rather than inert text is exactly what lets XSS execute in other visitors' browsers.
